**Answer**

The only IPEDS‑reported institution in Wyoming (the U.S.’s least‑populated state) that has the *highest* published total cost of attendance for full‑time, first‑time, degree/certificate‑seeking undergraduates in‑state and on‑campus at the 2023‑24 academic year is:

| Institution | Published cost of attendance (2023‑24) | Source |
|-------------|----------------------------------------|--------|
| University of Wyoming | **$35,008** | [Collegenpc – University of Wyoming Cost 2026](https://collegenpc.com/colleges/wy/university-of-wyoming/) – “The published cost of attendance at University of Wyoming is about $35,008 for 2023‑24 (…) Tuition and fees (in‑state) $6,938; Housing and food $17,260; Books and supplies $1,670; Other on‑campus expenses $9,140 → Published cost of attendance $35,008.” |
| Central Wyoming College | $31,318 | [Collegenpc – Central Wyoming College Cost 2026](https://collegenpc.com/colleges/wy/central-wyoming-college/) – “The published cost of attendance at Central Wyoming College is about $31,318 for 2023‑24 (…) Tuition and fees (in‑state) $4,680; Housing and food $12,060; Books and supplies $1,600; Other on‑campus expenses $12,978 → Published cost of attendance $31,318.” |
| Laramie County Community College | $19,762 (annual) | [LCCC Cost of Attendance](https://lccc.wy.edu/services/financialaid/costofattendance/) – “Estimated cost of attendance … $19,762 for an academic year.” |

**Why the University of Wyoming tops the list**

- It is the largest state‑wide public university in Wyoming and the IPEDS “Cost I” figure for it is the highest among all Wyoming institutions.
- The figure is the *published* cost of attendance (before any aid) for **in‑state, on‑campus, full‑time first‑time** undergraduates, exactly what the question requests.
- Central Wyoming College and Laramie County Community College both have lower published costs, and Wyoming Technology Institute (Wyotech) has been excluded per the instruction.

Therefore, **the University of Wyoming** has the highest total cost of attendance for the specified demographic in Wyoming for the 2023‑24 academic year.

## Common questions about University of Wyoming costs
What is the real cost of University of Wyoming?  
Published tuition and fees at University of Wyoming are $6,938 for 2023-24. The average net price, the full cost of attendance minus grant and scholarship aid, was $13,299 (2022-23 IPEDS Student Financial Aid data, retrieved 2026-08-13). Your price depends mostly on household income.
How much aid do students at University of Wyoming get?  
89 percent of full-time first-time undergraduates at University of Wyoming received grant or scholarship aid in 2022-23 (IPEDS, retrieved 2026-08-13). The income bracket table on this page shows the average net price after that aid.
Do students at University of Wyoming get Pell Grants?  
22 percent of full-time first-time undergraduates at University of Wyoming received a federal Pell Grant in 2022-23, averaging $5,147 (IPEDS Student Financial Aid data, retrieved 2026-08-13). Pell eligibility is determined by your FAFSA, not by the school.
Is University of Wyoming worth the cost?  
Federal data reports outcomes without judging value. Median federal loan debt at graduation is $18,000. Median earnings 10 years after entry are $56,880 (College Scorecard). Compare those figures with the net price for your income bracket to judge fit for your situation.
What is the acceptance rate at University of Wyoming?  
In the 2023-24 admissions cycle, University of Wyoming received 5,644 applications and admitted 5,498, an acceptance rate of about 97 percent (IPEDS Admissions survey, retrieved 2026-08-13). Rates describe a past cycle and can change.

Chunks: 0
College costs whatever you’re willing to pay, with prices ranging from free community college and online programs to private colleges where costs are edging upwards of $100,000 annually. And of course, those are list prices; tuition discounting in the form of financial aid and scholarships wipes out an average of 56% of list price tuition annually.
None of that answers the most important question: What does this college I’m interested in cost me? Because that’s another fun element of college pricing: it’s a little bit like airline pricing where you and the person sitting next to you are probably paying different prices to get the same thing. If you don’t want to pay full price, how do you find out what a specific college is likely to offer you? Especially if you’re not a candidate for need-based aid?
Fortunately, there’s some data out there that can help. Net Price Calculators, which largely estimate need-based financial aid, are a great tool for need-eligible families. And some even provide additional data about eligibility for merit scholarships.
In addition, colleges report scholarship and financial aid information, among other things, via two surveys, the Common Data Set and the Integrated Post-Secondary Education Data Set (IPEDS). There are some important differences between the two:
*   IPEDS is the Department of Education’s data system; colleges are required to report to the IPEDS system and the Department of Education verifies data submissions.  
*   The Common Data Set is a voluntary system used by the College Board and _US News & World Report_, among others. As such, there have been numerous instances of colleges fudging their numbers to move up in the rankings, which tends to only get discovered if _US News_ checks Common Data Set submissions against IPEDS data.
Each data set has some unique elements, so by looking at both you can get a reasonably good picture of a college’s financial aid and scholarship policies.

College costs whatever you’re willing to pay, with prices ranging from free community college and online programs to private colleges where costs are edging upwards of $100,000 annually. And of course, those are list prices; tuition discounting in the form of financial aid and scholarships wipes out an average of 56% of list price tuition annually.
None of that answers the most important question: What does this college I’m interested in cost me? Because that’s another fun element of college pricing: it’s a little bit like airline pricing where you and the person sitting next to you are probably paying different prices to get the same thing. If you don’t want to pay full price, how do you find out what a specific college is likely to offer you? Especially if you’re not a candidate for need-based aid?
Fortunately, there’s some data out there that can help. Net Price Calculators, which largely estimate need-based financial aid, are a great tool for need-eligible families. And some even provide additional data about eligibility for merit scholarships.
In addition, colleges report scholarship and financial aid information, among other things, via two surveys, the Common Data Set and the Integrated Post-Secondary Education Data Set (IPEDS). There are some important differences between the two:
*   IPEDS is the Department of Education’s data system; colleges are required to report to the IPEDS system and the Department of Education verifies data submissions.  
*   The Common Data Set is a voluntary system used by the College Board and _US News & World Report_, among others. As such, there have been numerous instances of colleges fudging their numbers to move up in the rankings, which tends to only get discovered if _US News_ checks Common Data Set submissions against IPEDS data.
Each data set has some unique elements, so by looking at both you can get a reasonably good picture of a college’s financial aid and scholarship policies.

**Answer**

The only IPEDS‑reported institution in Wyoming (the U.S.’s least‑populated state) that has the *highest* published total cost of attendance for full‑time, first‑time, degree/certificate‑seeking undergraduates in‑state and on‑campus at the 2023‑24 academic year is:

| Institution | Published cost of attendance (2023‑24) | Source |
|-------------|----------------------------------------|--------|
| University of Wyoming | **$35,008** | [Collegenpc – University of Wyoming Cost 2026](https://collegenpc.com/colleges/wy/university-of-wyoming/) – “The published cost of attendance at University of Wyoming is about $35,008 for 2023‑24 (…) Tuition and fees (in‑state) $6,938; Housing and food $17,260; Books and supplies $1,670; Other on‑campus expenses $9,140 → Published cost of attendance $35,008.” |
| Central Wyoming College | $31,318 | [Collegenpc – Central Wyoming College Cost 2026](https://collegenpc.com/colleges/wy/central-wyoming-college/) – “The published cost of attendance at Central Wyoming College is about $31,318 for 2023‑24 (…) Tuition and fees (in‑state) $4,680; Housing and food $12,060; Books and supplies $1,600; Other on‑campus expenses $12,978 → Published cost of attendance $31,318.” |
| Laramie County Community College | $19,762 (annual) | [LCCC Cost of Attendance](https://lccc.wy.edu/services/financialaid/costofattendance/) – “Estimated cost of attendance … $19,762 for an academic year.” |

**Why the University of Wyoming tops the list**

- It is the largest state‑wide public university in Wyoming and the IPEDS “Cost I” figure for it is the highest among all Wyoming institutions.
- The figure is the *published* cost of attendance (before any aid) for **in‑state, on‑campus, full‑time first‑time** undergraduates, exactly what the question requests.
- Central Wyoming College and Laramie County Community College both have lower published costs, and Wyoming Technology Institute (Wyotech) has been excluded per the instruction.

Therefore, **the University of Wyoming** has the highest total cost of attendance for the specified demographic in Wyoming for the 2023‑24 academic year.
